book_title: Chapter 8: Reading the Tape — Trend, Volume & Momentum Opportunity
question: Is the stock in a healthy uptrend, who is buying it and in what size, and is there a trade worth taking at ₹1,458.40 or only after the price comes back?

epigraph.quote: There is the plain fool, who does the wrong thing at all times everywhere, but there is the Wall Street fool, who thinks he must trade all the time.
epigraph.author: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator, 1923

web_blocks.text: The trend is real, and by the conventional test it is in Stage 2. Stan Weinstein's stage method asks one thing of a stock: is it above a rising 30-week average, and are the shorter averages stacked above it? At the 13 November 2026 close of ₹1,458.40, CNL sits 52.1% above its 30-week simple average of ₹958.91, which has itself risen about 10% in four weeks. It is above the 10-week exponential average (₹1,202.33), the 50-day average (₹1,160.36) and the 200-day average (₹863.29), the last by 68.9% [43]. The third-party stage screen counts 20 weeks in Stage 2 with a gain of 76.9% over that spell and a relative-strength reading of +21.0 [43]. The all-time closing high is ₹1,475.00 on 12 November, and the intraday high was ₹1,550.20 the same day [43]. In plain terms: the stock is in a confirmed uptrend that is young by Stage 2 standards (20 weeks) and stretched by any standard.

web_blocks.takeaway: Trend indicators are as strong as they get, while the momentum and volatility gauges say the move is stretched and noisy. This is a trend to respect, not a price to chase. [43]

web_blocks.text: Read the ledger as three timeframes pointing the same direction at different speeds. The weekly chart has the strongest evidence and the highest RSI. The daily chart is strong with room left. The four-hour chart shows a market that has stopped rising for a few days. The 12 November session reached ₹1,550.20 and closed at ₹1,475.00 (4.9% below the high). The 13 November session closed at ₹1,458.40 on 14,339 shares [43]. The width of the Bollinger bands, 41.97%, matters for how you read the pattern. A squeeze is a narrow band where price coils quietly before a breakout. A wide band is the opposite: a market that has already moved a long way quickly. CNL is in the second state, so the setups that work after a squeeze (a tight base with falling volume) do not apply today.

web_blocks.title: How stretched is it, and what has stretching meant for this stock?

web_blocks.text: The close is 21.3% above the 10-week exponential average, 25.7% above the 50-day average and 52.1% above the 30-week average [43]. We tested what such extension has meant in this stock's own history, using Friday closes since the 2017 listing. A week with the close at least 20% over the 10-week EMA occurred 38 times in 486 weeks, in eight separate episodes including this one. Seven of them have a 13-week follow-through we can read, and the verdict is mixed rather than decisive.

web_blocks.caption: Episodes since 2017 when the weekly close was 20% or more above the 10-week EMA (first week of each episode; weekly closes; Yahoo Finance bars)
headers: Worst weekly close in the next 13 weeks
web_blocks.takeaway: Four of the seven earlier episodes were higher after 13 weeks and three were lower by 6% to 22%. Extension is not a sell signal in this stock, but it has been followed by a dip of 8% or more in four of seven cases. [43]

web_blocks.text: Across all 36 qualifying weeks with a 13-week follow-through, 61% were higher 13 weeks later (median +13.2%), but only 47% were higher 26 weeks later (median −2.8%). The median worst dip in the following 13 weeks was −6.9% on weekly closes. In 39% of the weeks the dip was 11% or more, which is what a pullback to the top of the zone at ₹1,297.52 would be. One in four saw a dip of 17% or more, which would reach the 10-week average. And 14% saw a 20% fall. The 2021 episode, which carried the stock from ₹134 to ₹746, is the reason to respect the trend. The three losing episodes are the reason to respect the extension. Note that 18 of the 38 qualifying weeks come from the single 2021-22 run, so the history is shorter than the count suggests. Our judgement is that the odds of a pullback of 10% or more over the next three months are about two in five. On this stock's own record, the odds of a deep one (a fall of 20% or more) are about one in seven.

Volume tells you whether a move is being paid for. The 30-day average is 39,778 shares a day, about ₹5.8 Cr, and the 10-day average is 54,625 [43]. The big sessions came on the news. On 29 October 240,412 shares traded (6.0 times the 30-day average). On 4 November 229,638 traded (5.8 times), the day the stock cleared its August high of ₹1,328.00 with a 17.0% gain [43]. Since 12 August the up days have averaged 54,417 shares and the down days 23,915. That is the pattern of accumulation: buyers show up on rising days, and sellers do not on falling ones [43]. The weakness is in the last sessions. The 11 November rise of 9.5% came on 58,241 shares. The 6 and 9 November sessions traded 18,640 and 9,721 shares, and the 13 November close was on 14,339, 0.36 times the average [43]. A rally that stalls on low volume is resting, not being sold, but it has also not been confirmed.

The July volumes do not read as accumulation. On 9 July, 13 July, 24 July and 27 July the exchange bars show 34.3 lakh, 21.1 lakh, 56.5 lakh and 20.3 lakh shares. A normal day is 40,000 [43]. The bulk-deal tape lists nine trading firms on 24 July (including Microcurves, Junomoneta, NK Securities, QE Securities and Silverleaf) and three on 27 July. Each appeared on both the buy and the sell side of the same day at almost identical prices [54]. That is intraday round-tripping by trading desks, which inflates volume without a change in ownership. One intraday report put 24 July turnover at ₹149 Cr, which is 26 days of the current average value [54]. The lesson is that high-volume days in this stock include noise. The volume that counts is the delivered kind, which the exchange data in our snapshot does not isolate.

web_blocks.caption: How big a position is, relative to what trades (₹1,458.40 per share; volumes from TradingView and Yahoo Finance bars)
web_blocks.takeaway: A ₹10 lakh to ₹25 lakh order is small against a good day and large against a quiet one. On the 20% of the last 60 sessions with fewer than 10,000 shares traded, a ₹25 lakh sale would be at least 17% of the day. [43]

web_blocks.text: Who owns the stock matters because it decides who can sell. Promoters hold 56.62%, unchanged since September 2025. FIIs hold 0.48% (₹10.5 Cr at today's price), up from 0.27% in June. DIIs hold 2.23% (₹48.8 Cr), up from 1.28%. The public holds 40.67%, about ₹891 Cr at the current price, spread over 10,135 shareholders (up 11.8% in the September quarter) [44]. Institutions together own 2.7% of the company. That is too small to cushion a fall and large enough that a single fund's exit would show up on the tape. The shareholding filing for the December quarter, due in January, will reveal who bought the November move. Until then, the 11.8% rise in the number of holders in the September quarter says retail participation widened during the summer leg. That was before the October to November run [44].

The surveillance label is the most practical fact in this chapter. The snapshot tags CNL as under NSE's long-term additional surveillance measure, Stage II [43]. Under NSE's published framework, Stage I imposes a 100% margin from the third day after shortlisting. Stage II adds a cut of the price band to the next lower level while keeping the 100% margin [52]. Secondary guides add that this blocks intraday and leveraged trading, so every buyer must pay in full and take delivery. They also say that a stock stays in the framework for at least 90 calendar days before a weekly review can step it down one stage [52]. The bars show the band change. On 4 November the stock touched ₹1,421.60, exactly 20.0% over the prior close of ₹1,184.70. On 11 November it touched ₹1,472.60, exactly 10.0% over the prior ₹1,338.80, so the daily limit fell from 20% to 10% between those dates [43]. We could not find the entry date or stage history in NSE's circulars, so the date is an inference from the price bars. The measure is a surveillance step on trading patterns and not an adverse finding about the company [52]. For you it means fewer speculative buyers and no intraday exits. It also brings a risk the chart does not show: on a bad day with a 10% band, sell orders can lock the stock at the lower limit and trap holders for sessions.

web_blocks.title: Gaps, shelves and where the price has already been

web_blocks.text: The popular story is that the stock gapped up in July and August and again in November. The bars say otherwise. The rises came as intraday surges on news and volume, not as clean gaps. There are only two true gaps (a day whose low is above the prior day's high) since June. The first was on 8 June: a gap of +20.0% at the open, with the day's low of ₹712.75 above the prior high of ₹648.00. It followed the BSNL BharatNet announcement over the weekend. The second was a trivial one on 12 August [43]. The June gap was partly refilled on 12 June to ₹691.00 and has not been revisited since. The zone from ₹648.00 to ₹691.00 is old support the market has left far behind. The July surges (9, 13, 24 and 27 July) and the 4 November breakout all opened within 4.4% of the prior close and ran from there [43]. What the chart does hold are shelves: places where price spent weeks and where buyers and sellers have already made decisions.

The scanner's support zone, bracketing the 20-day EMA (1,278.34), 10-week EMA (1,202.33) and 50-day EMA (1,181.84) [43]

web_blocks.takeaway: There is no strong shelf between ₹1,328 and ₹1,550 to catch a fall, and none at all below the ₹1,184 to ₹1,298 zone until ₹975. The zone is where the chart's support is concentrated, and the 12-week base behind it (high ₹1,328, low ₹975, 26.6% deep) is where the next decision point sits. [43]

web_blocks.text: The base from 12 August to 3 November is worth a closer look. It ran for 57 sessions, with a high of ₹1,328.00 (31 August) and a low of ₹975.00 (23 October), a depth of 26.6%. Average volume was 36,074 shares a day [43]. A 27% base is deep and untidy by Stage 2 standards; it is a correction inside a young uptrend, not a quiet coil. The breakout on 4 November came on 5.8 times average volume. The retest of the old high on 6 November held exactly on the line (low ₹1,300.20, close ₹1,327.90) on 18,640 shares, which is the textbook behaviour of a breakout that is genuine. The breakout is 1.3 weeks old. It has not yet built a new base above ₹1,328, so there is no fresh pivot to buy against, only the old shelf 8.9% below.

web_blocks.title: Relative strength: CNL against the market and its peers

web_blocks.caption: Price performance to 13 November 2026 (stocks per TradingView; Nifty 50 from Yahoo Finance daily closes over approximately the same windows)
rows: Relative-strength reading of the stage screen
Weinstein stage (snapshot evaluation; ledger shows Redington and Rashi in Stage 3)
web_blocks.takeaway: CNL has beaten the index by 25 percentage points in a month and about 115 over a year, and it is the only name in the group still rising over the last month. The stock is moving on its own story, not on a sector tide. [43][45]

web_blocks.text: The peer picture is two-sided. The good news is that CNL leads the one-month, three-month and six-month windows and trails only CP Plus (+164%) over one year, against +112% for CNL and +106% for Rashi, which shows a strong year for the wider group. The bad news is that the group's momentum has broken. Redington is down 10.3% over the month and in Stage 3. Rashi is down 22.1% in a month and 15.9% in the last week, and sits in a downtrend (Stage 4 on the snapshot evaluation, Stage 3 on the daily ledger). CP Plus is down 5.2% [43][45]. The stage screen lists 100% Stage 2 density for its Distributor and Stockists group. That reads as a one-name sample, since the two largest listed distributors are both in Stage 3 on the daily ledger, and Rashi reads Stage 4 on the snapshot evaluation. The sector tailwind is therefore not evidenced [43]. A stock that rises alone, as CNL has in the last month, has idiosyncratic support (the Infinova, Zicom and AT&T news) and idiosyncratic risk. When the story cracks, there is no sector bid to catch it. The AT&T filing, for instance, gave the stock a 5.7% intraday spike and a close only 0.6% higher [51][54].

CNL is not in NSE's futures and options segment, so there is no listed options chain and the options screen returns NOT_OPTIONABLE_OR_ILLIQUID [43]. Any view on the stock has to be expressed in cash equity, and with the surveillance margin in force that means paying in full. That removes the usual ways to define risk with a premium (buying a call, selling a put). The only risk control is the stop, the position size and the choice of entry price.

web_blocks.title: The realistic short-term trading edge, and the conditions that would create one

web_blocks.text: At ₹1,458.40 the stock offers no good short-term entry. The top of the support zone is 11.0% below the price, and the price is 5.9% below the high. It is extended on every measure, and the 4H turn is false. The last session traded on 0.36 times the average volume. A stop at the nearest meaningful support, the 10-week EMA at ₹1,202.33, is 17.6% below the price. A trade needs a stop that is close enough to keep the loss tolerable and far enough not to be hit by an ordinary ₹90 day. Today those two requirements conflict. There are two setups that would fix that, and neither exists yet. The first is a pullback into the ₹1,202 to ₹1,298 zone, where the 20-day EMA, the 10-week EMA and the 50-day EMA stack up. Volume should dry up on the way, below the 39,778-share average on the down days, which has been the pattern since August. The second is a new base above ₹1,550.20 that holds for three to five weeks within a 10% to 15% range. It would then need a weekly close above ₹1,550.20 on rising volume. By our reading of the history above, the first has about a 40% chance of occurring in the next 13 weeks and the second a lower one, perhaps 25%. That is a judgement from the stock's own past and not a forecast.

Two ATRs below the zone top (2 × ₹90.23)
Beyond the noise of ordinary daily swings; a volatility-based stop [43]
The medium-term trend has turned from rising to flat or falling [43]

web_blocks.takeaway: A stop of 7% to 14% below the zone top fits a tactical trade. A stop at the 30-week average is a position-holder's stop and costs 26% to 34%, which is why the entry price decides whether the trade makes sense at all. [43]

web_blocks.title: Real-World Walkthrough 1: placing a ₹25 lakh order on 13 November
paragraphs: The investor. A portfolio manager wants a ₹25 lakh position, 1,714 shares at ₹1,458.40, after reading the AT&T announcement. The stock closed 1.1% lower on the day with 14,339 shares traded, so the whole position equals 12% of the day's volume. [43]

The order. The stock is under surveillance with a 100% margin. The buyer must have the full ₹25 lakh in the account and cannot trade out of it the same day. A market order would sweep several price levels on a thin book. So the buyer works a limit order over two or three sessions at the price he is willing to pay. [52]

The risk after the fill. A stop at the 10-week EMA is ₹256 a share away, a loss of about ₹4.4 lakh, or 17.6% of the position. An ordinary ATR day moves the position ₹1.55 lakh. On a bad day with a 10% band, a seller may find the stock locked at the lower limit for a session. [43][52]

What it means. The stock is tradeable, the trend is real, and the position is small enough to enter and exit in a few sessions. The cost of being early is that the risk is large relative to the stop distance. The cost of waiting for the zone is that the stock may not return. That trade-off is the whole decision.

web_blocks.text: The technical timing gate for this stock reads CAP_WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT. The trend is strong enough to keep the stock on the list and extended enough that the tape gives no edge at ₹1,458.40. The reward in the base case is below the market, the stop distance is large against the ordinary daily swing, volume is thin, and the surveillance regime narrows the exits. The gate would open on a pullback into the ₹1,184 to ₹1,298 zone with falling volume. It would also open on a weekly close above ₹1,550.20 after a proper base. It would close, for any holder, on a weekly close below the 30-week average at ₹958.91. How the gate combines with the valuation and the business-quality evidence is for Chapter 9.

book_paragraphs: Let me start with the question beginners usually skip: what does it mean for a stock to be in an uptrend? Stan Weinstein's answer is simple and I like it. Look at a 30-week average, the price over six months of Fridays, and ask two things: is the average rising, and is the price above it? CNL's 30-week average is ₹958.91 and rising about 10% a month; the price is ₹1,458.40, which is 52% above it. The stock has been in Stage 2 for 20 weeks and has gained 77% in that spell. When I look at that chart, I see an uptrend that is real. I also see one that is only five months old, in a market that has handed the stock a doubling in six. Real and young is a good combination for a position, and a poor one for a purchase today.

Now let me show you the rubber band. The price is 21.3% above its 10-week average and 25.7% above the 50-day, and I wanted to know what that has meant before. So I went back through every Friday since the 2017 listing, and found eight episodes of stretch like this one. Of the seven we can read, four were higher 13 weeks later and three were lower by 6% to 22%. Across all the qualifying weeks, 39% of the time the stock gave back 11% or more over the next three months, which is exactly the distance from here to the top of the support zone. One in four fell 17% or more. A stretched rubber band is not a signal to sell. It is a reminder that a decline of a tenth is an ordinary event in this stock, not a crisis.

Volume is the part of the tape that is hardest to fake, so let me tell you how I read it. On 29 October and 4 November the stock traded about six times its normal volume on the way up, which is what a real breakout looks like. Since August the up days have averaged 54,417 shares and the down days 23,915, so buyers have been showing up when it matters and sellers have not. Then look at the last few sessions. The 11 November rally came on 58,241 shares, 6 November on 18,640 and 9 November on 9,721. On the last day, 14,339 shares traded, 0.36 times the average. Think of a street with fewer and fewer people walking along it. The street may still be going somewhere, but you would want to know who is left.

Let me put a rupee figure on thin liquidity, because this is where beginners get hurt. Suppose you want ₹25 lakh of this stock. At ₹1,458.40 that is 1,714 shares, and 4.3% of a normal day's volume, which sounds harmless. But half the time a normal day is closer to 20,000 shares, so your order is 8.5% of the whole market for the day, and on a quiet day with 10,000 shares it is 17%. Imagine a warehouse with one narrow door. A single pallet goes through easily, and fifty pallets arrive at the same time as everyone else. A ₹10 lakh order is a pallet; a ₹25 lakh order is a trolley. Neither is a problem going in. Both can be a problem when the whole street is trying to leave.

The surveillance label is the fact that changes how you can trade. NSE has put CNL in its long-term additional surveillance framework, Stage II. In plain terms, you must pay 100% of the value to buy it, you cannot trade it out the same day, and the daily price limit has been cut in half. I checked the bars and the cut shows: on 4 November the stock touched exactly 20% above the previous close, and on 11 November exactly 10%. That sounds like a nuisance and it is a risk. If bad news arrives, sellers can find the stock locked at the lower limit for a session or two, and the price you thought you could exit at is not available. NSE says surveillance is not a comment on the company. I believe that, and I would still plan for it.

Now the four-hour, daily and weekly charts, and why I look at all three. The weekly RSI is 72.96, above the 70 line that marks a stretched market. The daily RSI is 67.11, and the four-hour is 66.32. All three say the same thing at different speeds: strong, a little tired. The Bollinger band width is 41.97%, which tells you volatility has expanded with the move. Many people expect a calm, tight base before a breakout; here we have the reverse, a market that went up fast and wide. And the four-hour chart has not turned. When a stretched stock stops rising, the first sign of a pause appears on the short chart, and that sign is not there yet. The market is neither rolling over nor consolidating; it is simply waiting.

You may have read that the stock gapped up in July and August. It did not, quite, and I want you to see why this matters. A gap is a hole in the chart, a day when the stock opens above the previous day's high and never trades below it, and holes tend to attract price later. I checked every bar since June and found just two: 8 June, after the BharatNet news, and a trivial one in August. The big July and November days opened near the previous close and ran, which leaves no hole to fall into. What the chart does show are shelves. Between ₹1,184 and ₹1,298 sit the 20-day, 10-week and 50-day averages together. Below that, the next real support is ₹975. If you ask me where a decline would find buyers, I would point to that zone, and I would point out that there is nothing underneath it for a long way.

Then there is the question of who the stock is rising with. Over the last month CNL is up 36%, Redington is down 10%, Rashi Peripherals is down 22% and CP Plus is down 5%. The stock is not riding a wave; it is the wave. The chairman said on the October call, “Demand is tremendous because AI has really, really made our current infrastructure redundant,” and the market has paid for that sentence. But a stock that rises alone has idiosyncratic support and idiosyncratic risk. When the story is Infinova, Zicom and AT&T, the story can change with one filing. And the volume in July reminds me not to count every busy day as a crowd: nine trading firms were on both sides of the bulk-deal tape on 24 July. Desks make volume. Owners make a base.

So what is the realistic short-term trade? I will be plain about it: at ₹1,458.40 I do not see one that has a good edge. The nearest support worth the name is the 10-week average at ₹1,202, which is 17.6% down. A stop that far is bigger than most traders can stomach, and a stop that is near enough is smaller than a normal ₹90 day. That conflict is what an extended stock looks like. Two things would change my mind. One is a pullback into the ₹1,202 to ₹1,298 zone on drying volume, the sort of fall that followed about 39% of the stretched weeks in this stock's history. The other is a new, tight base above ₹1,550 that holds for a few weeks and breaks out on rising volume.

Let me talk about stops, because a stop is the only protection you have in a stock with no options. A stop belongs where the story would be wrong, not where the loss would be comfortable. If you buy at the top of the zone, ₹1,297.52, a weekly close below the 10-week average at ₹1,202 says the pause is longer than normal and costs about 7%. Two daily ranges below the zone top is ₹1,117, 14% away. A close below the 30-week average at ₹958.91 would end Stage 2 by definition, and is 26% below the zone top. Match the stop to the horizon: the nearer ones for a trader, the 30-week average for someone who plans to hold. And remember that in a 10% band market a stop is a wish, not a guarantee.

I should also tell you what you cannot do here. CNL is not in the futures and options segment, so there is no call to buy and no put to sell. You have cash equity and you have patience. Putting it all together, the technical gate for the stock reads CAP_WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT, which is the scanner's way of saying that the trend is good enough to keep watching and the price is too stretched to hand over capital without a better entry. I agree with the reading. The gate opens on a pullback into the zone on thin volume, or on a weekly close above ₹1,550.20 after a base. It shuts for anyone who holds if the 30-week average goes. What to do with all that, with the valuation and the quality of the business, is the job of Chapter 9.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: I have watched many stocks like this one, and the mistake that costs most is not buying late; it is mistaking a good company's chart for a good entry. The trend here is real and has the volume to prove it on the days that mattered. The price, today, is simply a long way from where anyone with a stop could sleep. The right feeling is neither fear nor greed. It is the patience of someone who knows the stock will give a second chance, or will not, and who has decided in advance which of the two is acceptable.

book_callouts.title: THE STOP-DISTANCE TEST
book_callouts.text: Before any trade, write down two numbers: the distance to a stop that would prove you wrong, and the size of an ordinary day's move. If the stop is closer than one ordinary day, you will be shaken out by noise; if it is further than you can afford to lose, the entry is wrong, not the stop. In CNL today the stop that makes sense is 17.6% away and the ordinary day is 6.2%. When the test fails, the answer is to wait for a better entry, not to move the stop.
